women seafarer recruitment and retention policies and practices are in need of improvement, and that women seafaring is not as difficult as it is perceived to be by the industry.

the issue of the recruitment, retention and utilization of women seafarer in the context of the predicted labour shortage in shipping and the need to attract and retain a diverse and skilled labour force.
the question: how can the maritime labour market be made more gender equal and inclusive?
the issue of gender equality in the maritime industry, and the potential for women's participation in the labour market to contribute to solving the industry's labour shortage.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
women seafarer recruitment, retention and promotion are not only a matter of social justice but also a matter of business.
women seafaring is not only possible but is also a viable career choice.
the industry needs to be more open to employing women, to recognize their skills and abilities and to promote the recruitment of women into the industry.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the industry is not yet ready to employ women seafar-ers in large numbers.
women seafarer's are an underutilized resource.
there is no reason why more women should not be employed at sea and that, in fact, they should be encouraged to do so.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a real need for employers to be more open to the employment of women in sea-going jobs and to recognize their potential as a valuable source of skilled labour in the industry.

women seafarer employment should be encouraged and promoted by employers, unions, maritime authorities, maritime training institutes, seafarers' welfare bodies, maritime organizations, and governments.
